topics.name: Stamp Act
topics.kicker: 1765 British tax on printed paper · “No taxation without representation”
topics.briefing: In 1765, Parliament ordered American colonists to use specially marked, taxed paper for newspapers, legal documents, pamphlets, and even playing cards, to help pay for British troops in America. The colonies exploded in protest: crowds hanged tax collectors in effigy, the Sons of Liberty organized, nine colonies sent delegates to a special congress, and merchants stopped buying British goods. Parliament repealed the Stamp Act in 1766 but passed the Declaratory Act the same day, insisting it could still make laws for the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.”
topics.answerHtml: Stamp Act of 1765 (accept Duties in American Colonies Act; prompt on stamp tax; do not accept “Sugar Act,” “Townshend Acts,” or “Tea Act”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: During a debate over this law, Isaac Barré [“bah-RAY”], a member of Parliament who had fought in the French and Indian War, defended the colonists by saying that British oppression, not British care, had planted them in America. The city of Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, is named partly for him.
tossups.r: In that speech, Barré called the colonists “Sons of Liberty.” For 10 points, name this 1765 British tax on newspapers, legal papers, and playing cards.

tossups.p: On August 14, 1765, a Boston crowd hanged an effigy of Andrew Oliver from a large elm, later called the Liberty Tree, because he had been chosen to collect this law’s tax in Massachusetts. Oliver agreed to resign the next day, and less than two weeks later a mob wrecked the mansion of Lieutenant Governor Thomas Hutchinson.
tossups.r: Parliament repealed this law in 1766. For 10 points, name this tax that required colonists to buy specially marked paper.

tossups.p: In May 1765, a new member of Virginia’s House of Burgesses introduced resolutions declaring that only Virginia’s own assembly could tax Virginians. In a speech against this law, he reportedly warned that “Caesar had his Brutus” and that King George III might “profit by their example.”
tossups.r: That burgess was Patrick Henry. For 10 points, name this 1765 tax on printed paper, which led to the cry “No taxation without representation.”

tossups.p: In October 1765, delegates from nine colonies met at New York’s City Hall to protest this law, and they approved a Declaration of Rights and Grievances written mostly by John Dickinson. That meeting took its name from this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1765 law, proposed by George Grenville, that taxed newspapers and legal documents.

tossups.p: People accused of breaking this law could be tried in vice-admiralty courts, which had no juries, and its tax had to be paid in British currency rather than colonial paper money. Prime Minister George Grenville proposed it to help pay for about 10,000 British soldiers kept in North America.
tossups.r: Colonists protested it with the slogan “No taxation without representation.” For 10 points, name this 1765 tax on printed paper.

tossups.p: In February 1766, Benjamin Franklin told the House of Commons that the colonists would never pay this law’s tax unless they were forced to by arms. William Pitt also urged Parliament to repeal it, telling members that he rejoiced that America had resisted.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this tax that Parliament repealed in March 1766, the same day it passed the Declaratory Act.

tossups.p: On the same day in March 1766 that Parliament repealed this law, it passed an act declaring that it could make laws binding the colonies “in all cases whatsoever.” The government of the Marquess of Rockingham [“ROCK-ing-um”] carried out that repeal.
tossups.r: That act was the Declaratory Act. For 10 points, name this 1765 tax law, which sparked the cry “No taxation without representation.”

tossups.p: This law taxed dice and playing cards, along with diplomas, ship’s papers, almanacs, and pamphlets. It angered lawyers, printers, and merchants most of all, since their work used so much paper.
tossups.r: Newspapers and legal documents needed specially marked paper too. For 10 points, name this 1765 law proposed by George Grenville.

tossups.p: Merchants in New York, Philadelphia, and Boston agreed to stop importing British goods until this law was repealed, and British merchants who lost business then lobbied Parliament against it. Most of the officials chosen to distribute this law’s specially marked paper were pressured into resigning before it took effect on November 1, 1765.
tossups.r: Groups called the Sons of Liberty formed to fight it. For 10 points, name this 1765 British tax on printed paper.

tossups.p: Thomas Whately, a British official, defended this law by arguing that the colonists were “virtually represented” in Parliament even though they elected no members to it. In Massachusetts, John Adams wrote instructions for the town of Braintree protesting this law.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1765 law that colonists opposed with the cry “No taxation without representation.”

tossups.p: In Boston, a secret club of artisans and shopkeepers called the Loyal Nine organized the first protests against this law. A shoemaker named Ebenezer Mackintosh led the crowds that attacked the property of royal officials.
tossups.r: Groups called the Sons of Liberty soon formed in other colonies. For 10 points, name this 1765 tax on printed paper, repealed in 1766.

tossups.p: One year after the Sugar Act lowered the tax on molasses but enforced it more strictly, Parliament passed this law, the first direct tax it ever placed on the American colonies. A Quartering Act passed soon afterward required colonies to supply British troops with housing and supplies.
tossups.r: Colonists protested this law by boycotting British goods. For 10 points, name this 1765 tax on newspapers and legal documents.

tossups.p: Timothy Ruggles of Massachusetts presided over a congress that met to oppose this law, but he refused to sign its petitions, and his colony’s legislature later scolded him for it. James Otis had proposed calling that congress.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1765 British tax law, whose repeal came with the Declaratory Act.

tossups.p: Benjamin Franklin hurt his reputation at home by recommending his friend John Hughes to distribute this law’s specially marked paper in Pennsylvania. In September 1765, Franklin’s wife, Deborah, refused to leave their Philadelphia house and prepared to defend it when an angry crowd threatened it.
tossups.r: Franklin later testified against this law in Parliament. For 10 points, name this 1765 tax on printed paper.

tossups.p: Grateful New Yorkers voted to put up statues of King George III and William Pitt after Parliament repealed this law. Years later, after the Declaration of Independence was read in the city in July 1776, a crowd pulled down the king’s statue at Bowling Green.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1765 British tax on newspapers, legal documents, and playing cards.

trap.title: Which British tax?
trap.body: Parliament taxed the colonies several times before the Revolution. The Sugar Act (1764) taxed molasses, the Stamp Act (1765) taxed printed paper, the Townshend Acts (1767) taxed glass, lead, paint, paper, and tea brought into the colonies, and the Tea Act (1773) led to the Boston Tea Party. The Stamp Act Congress is its own answer line, so answering with the law when a question asks for “this meeting” or “this congress” is wrong.
trap.fix: Grenville, 1765, newspapers, playing cards, Andrew Oliver, Patrick Henry’s Virginia Resolves, and repeal alongside the Declaratory Act mean the Stamp Act. Molasses and 1764 mean the Sugar Act; glass, paint, and Charles Townshend mean the Townshend Acts.
trap.line: Real answer line: Stamp Act of 1765 (accept Duties in American Colonies Act; prompt on stamp tax; do not accept “Sugar Act,” “Townshend Acts,” or “Tea Act”)

topics.name: Seminoles
topics.kicker: Native nation of Florida · Fought three wars against the United States
topics.briefing: In the 1700s, Creek families and other Native people moved into Spanish Florida and formed a new nation, the Seminoles, who were allied with communities of Black people who had escaped slavery. They fought three wars against the United States, and the longest, in which Osceola was a famous war leader, lasted from 1835 to 1842. Most Seminoles were forced west to Indian Territory, but a few hundred stayed in the Everglades, and their descendants still live in Florida.
topics.answerHtml: Seminoles (or Seminole Nation; accept Seminole Tribe of Florida; prompt on Miccosukee, Black Seminoles, or Five Civilized Tribes; do not accept “Cherokee” or “Creek”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This people’s name is often traced to the Spanish word cimarrón [“see-mah-ROHN”], meaning “wild” or “runaway,” because their ancestors broke away from other nations and moved into Spanish lands. Many of those ancestors were Creek people from Georgia and Alabama who moved south in the 1700s.
tossups.r: Osceola was one of their most famous war leaders. For 10 points, name this Native nation of Florida.

tossups.p: In 1818, a U.S. general who had invaded Spanish Florida to fight this people captured St. Marks and Pensacola and executed two British subjects, Alexander Arbuthnot [“ar-BUTH-not”] and Robert Ambrister, whom he accused of helping them. The next year, Spain agreed to give Florida to the United States.
tossups.r: That general was Andrew Jackson. For 10 points, name this Native nation that fought three wars against the United States in Florida.

tossups.p: On December 28, 1835, warriors of this nation ambushed Major Francis Dade’s column of about 110 soldiers, and only a few soldiers survived. On the same day, a war leader of this nation killed the Indian agent Wiley Thompson outside Fort King.
tossups.r: That leader was Osceola. Those attacks began the second of three wars between this nation and the United States. For 10 points, name this nation of Florida.

tossups.p: In 1837, soldiers acting on General Thomas Jesup’s orders seized a war leader of this nation when he came to talk under a white flag of truce, and many Americans condemned the act. That leader, whose portrait was painted by George Catlin, died a few months later at Fort Moultrie in South Carolina.
tossups.r: That leader was Osceola. For 10 points, name this Native nation that fought the United States in Florida in the 1800s.

tossups.p: Under the 1823 Treaty of Moultrie Creek, this nation moved onto an inland reservation, but a later treaty signed at Payne’s Landing in 1832 called for its people to move west of the Mississippi River. Many of them said the leaders who signed that second treaty had no right to do so.
tossups.r: The dispute led to a long war. For 10 points, name this nation that resisted removal in Florida, led partly by Osceola.

tossups.p: John Horse, also called Juan Caballo [“HWAHN kah-BAH-yoh”], was a leader of this nation’s Black allies, many of whom had escaped slavery in Georgia and the Carolinas. In 1849 and 1850, he and the leader Wild Cat led a group of this nation’s people and their Black allies to northern Mexico.
tossups.r: Osceola fought for this nation in the 1830s. For 10 points, name this Native nation of Florida.

tossups.p: On Christmas Day 1837, Colonel Zachary Taylor’s army fought warriors of this nation at the Battle of Lake Okeechobee [“oh-kee-CHOH-bee”], one of the largest battles of a seven-year war. Leaders on the other side included Alligator and Abiaka [“ah-bee-AH-kah”], a medicine man also called Sam Jones.
tossups.r: Taylor later became president. For 10 points, name this nation of Florida, whose war leaders included Osceola.

tossups.p: The medicine man Abiaka [“ah-bee-AH-kah”], also called Sam Jones, never surrendered and led his followers deep into the Everglades, where soldiers could not catch them. This nation’s tribe there calls itself “unconquered,” and it is often said that it never signed a peace treaty with the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Native nation of Florida, which fought three wars against the United States.

tossups.p: In 1858, Billy Bowlegs, also known as Holata Micco [“hoh-LAH-tah MIK-oh”], agreed to move west with many of his followers, ending the last of three wars between his nation and the United States. That war had begun in 1855, after army surveyors damaged crops belonging to his band.
tossups.r: A few hundred of his people stayed in the Everglades. For 10 points, name this Native nation of Florida, whose war leaders included Osceola.

tossups.p: In November 1837, the war leader Wild Cat, also called Coacoochee [“koh-uh-KOO-chee”], and other prisoners from this nation squeezed through a narrow opening high in a wall of Fort Marion in St. Augustine and escaped. A more famous leader of this nation, who was held in the same fort, did not go with them.
tossups.r: That leader was Osceola. For 10 points, name this Native nation that resisted removal in the 1830s.

tossups.p: After their removal west, this nation’s people were at first made to settle on Creek land, but in 1856 they received a separate reservation of their own. Their nation’s capital in Oklahoma is Wewoka [“wee-WOH-kuh”].
tossups.r: Others stayed in Florida. For 10 points, name this nation, one of the “Five Civilized Tribes,” that was once led in war by Osceola.

tossups.p: In 2007, a tribe of this nation bought the Hard Rock Cafe company, a deal often described as the first purchase of a major international company by a Native American tribe. The separate Miccosukee [“mik-uh-SOO-kee”] Tribe, whose members share much of this nation’s history, was recognized by the U.S. government in 1962.
tossups.r: Florida State University’s teams use this nation’s name, with the tribe’s approval. For 10 points, name this Native nation, which fought three wars against the United States.

tossups.p: Members of this nation are known for colorful patchwork clothing sewn from narrow strips of cloth, and for chickees [“CHICK-eez”], open-sided houses with roofs thatched with palmetto leaves. Many of its people speak Mikasuki [“mih-KAH-soo-kee”] or the Muscogee language.
tossups.r: Their 1830s war leaders included Osceola. For 10 points, name this Native nation of Florida.

tossups.p: In 1816, U.S. forces destroyed a fort on the Apalachicola [“ap-uh-lach-ih-KOH-luh”] River that had been held by Black people who had escaped slavery, along with some Native allies. That attack, and clashes over the next year, helped lead to the first of three wars between this nation and the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Native nation, later led in war by Osceola, that lived in Florida.

tossups.p: Generals including Winfield Scott and Thomas Jesup commanded U.S. forces against this nation in a war from 1835 to 1842, often called the longest and costliest war the United States ever fought against a Native nation. That war followed the Indian Removal Act of 1830.
tossups.r: Osceola led many of its warriors. For 10 points, name this Native nation that resisted removal from Florida.

trap.title: Which Southeastern nation?
trap.body: The Seminole, Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, and Chickasaw were all called the “Five Civilized Tribes,” and all were forced west in the 1800s, so their clues blur together. The Seminoles grew partly out of the Creek, but answering “Creek” or “Cherokee” is wrong when the clues point to Florida. The three wars are separate answer lines, so naming the people when a question asks for “this war” loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Florida, the Everglades, Osceola, Dade’s battle, Billy Bowlegs, and Andrew Jackson’s 1818 invasion mean the Seminoles. Sequoyah, John Ross, and New Echota mean the Cherokee; the Red Sticks and Horseshoe Bend mean the Creek. Listen for “this nation” versus “this war.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Seminoles (or Seminole Nation; accept Seminole Tribe of Florida; prompt on Miccosukee, Black Seminoles, or Five Civilized Tribes; do not accept “Cherokee” or “Creek”)

topics.name: Shays’ Rebellion
topics.kicker: Massachusetts farmers’ revolt, 1786–1787 · Exposed the Articles’ weakness
topics.briefing: In 1786, farmers in western Massachusetts were losing their land, and some were even jailed, because they could not pay their debts and the state’s heavy taxes, which had to be paid in gold or silver. Led partly by Daniel Shays, a veteran of the Revolution, they shut down courts and in January 1787 marched on the federal arsenal at Springfield, where militia cannons drove them off. The uprising scared many leaders into pushing for a stronger national government at the Constitutional Convention that summer.
topics.answerHtml: Shays’ Rebellion (or Shays’s Rebellion; prompt on Shays; do not accept “Whiskey Rebellion”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Rebels in this uprising wore sprigs of hemlock in their hats and called themselves “Regulators,” and many of them were veterans of the Revolutionary War. They began by closing county courts in towns such as Northampton to stop judges from taking farms for unpaid debts.
tossups.r: Its best-known leader was a former army captain from Pelham. For 10 points, name this Massachusetts revolt of 1786 and 1787 led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: Writing from Paris, Thomas Jefferson responded to this uprising by telling James Madison that “a little rebellion now and then is a good thing.” Abigail Adams, writing from London, took a harsher view, calling its participants “ignorant, restless desperadoes.”
tossups.r: This revolt pushed many leaders to support a stronger national government. For 10 points, name this uprising led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: A message from Luke Day saying that his men would attack a day late was intercepted, so the main force of this uprising marched without them. On January 25, 1787, General William Shepard’s militia fired cannons at that force near the federal arsenal at Springfield, killing four men.
tossups.r: That defeat was the turning point of this uprising. For 10 points, name this revolt of Massachusetts farmers led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: After an overnight march through a snowstorm, General Benjamin Lincoln’s army surprised and scattered the main force of this uprising at Petersham in February 1787. Lincoln’s army had been paid for by wealthy Boston merchants, because the national government could not afford to raise troops.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rebellion, led by Daniel Shays, that showed the weakness of the Articles of Confederation.

tossups.p: Before this uprising, a state government raised taxes sharply to pay off its war debts and required that they be paid in gold or silver coin, which few farmers in the state’s western hills had. Farmers who could not pay lost their land in court or were sent to debtors’ prison.
tossups.r: Governor James Bowdoin [“BOH-din”] sent the militia to stop it. For 10 points, name this 1786–1787 rebellion of Massachusetts farmers led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: Henry Knox, the national Secretary at War, sent George Washington an alarming report claiming that the rebels in this uprising wanted all property to be shared in common. Fear of this uprising helped persuade Washington to come out of retirement and travel to Philadelphia in 1787.
tossups.r: It was put down by state militia in early 1787. For 10 points, name this revolt of Massachusetts farmers led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: After this uprising, voters replaced Governor James Bowdoin [“BOH-din”] with John Hancock, who had held the office before and who pardoned many of its participants. Hancock’s government also lowered taxes and gave some relief to people in debt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this revolt of Massachusetts farmers in 1786 and 1787, led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: In September 1786, the Annapolis Convention called for a meeting the next year to fix the national government, and news of this uprising over the following months convinced more states to send delegates. The Confederation Congress could not raise an army to stop it.
tossups.r: The Massachusetts militia ended it in 1787. For 10 points, name this revolt of indebted farmers led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: In a letter to James Madison, George Washington asked, “What stronger evidence can be given of the want of energy in our governments than these disorders?” Washington was writing about this uprising, in which armed crowds forced courts to close in the fall of 1786.
tossups.r: Its rebels were mostly farmers from western Massachusetts. For 10 points, name this rebellion led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: During this uprising, the state legislature passed a Riot Act and suspended the writ of habeas corpus [“HAY-bee-us KOR-pus”] so that suspected leaders could be held without trial. One of those leaders, Job Shattuck, was captured in late 1786.
tossups.r: Its best-known leader was Daniel Shays. For 10 points, name this 1786–1787 uprising in Massachusetts.

tossups.p: After this uprising collapsed in February 1787, its best-known leader fled to Vermont, which was then an independent republic outside the United States. A last clash came that month at Sheffield, in the far southwestern corner of the state where the uprising began.
tossups.r: That leader was Daniel Shays. For 10 points, name this rebellion of indebted farmers in western Massachusetts.

tossups.p: Partly in response to this uprising, the U.S. Constitution lets Congress call out the militia to “suppress Insurrections” and promises federal protection to the states against “domestic Violence.” Under the old system, Congress had no power to collect taxes or raise troops on its own to stop it.
tossups.r: The state militia ended it in early 1787. For 10 points, name this 1786–1787 revolt in western Massachusetts led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: Unlike the later Whiskey Rebellion, this uprising was put down by state militia rather than a national army, since the Confederation Congress could not raise one. Its leaders had asked for paper money and for laws that would delay the collection of debts.
tossups.r: It had begun in 1786 when farmers closed courts in western Massachusetts. For 10 points, name this rebellion led by Daniel Shays.

tossups.p: The leader of this uprising had risen to the rank of captain in the Continental Army during the Revolution, and like many of his followers, he came home deep in debt. He lived in the hill town of Pelham, east of the Connecticut River.
tossups.r: That captain was Daniel Shays. For 10 points, name the uprising that he led in western Massachusetts in 1786 and 1787.

tossups.p: Merchants in Boston who owed money to British lenders demanded hard money from country storekeepers, who in turn sued farmers, setting off the debt crisis behind this uprising. Western farmers also resented a state legislature that they saw as run by eastern merchants.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1786–1787 revolt led by Daniel Shays, which helped lead to the Constitutional Convention.

trap.title: Shays’ or Whiskey?
trap.body: Two early farmers’ revolts against taxes are easy to mix up. Shays’ Rebellion (1786–1787) was in western Massachusetts under the Articles of Confederation and was ended by state militia; the Whiskey Rebellion (1791–1794) was in western Pennsylvania against Alexander Hamilton’s tax on whiskey and ended when George Washington sent a federal army. Saying only “Shays” earns a prompt, since Daniel Shays is a person, not an event.
trap.fix: Massachusetts, Springfield, Benjamin Lincoln, hemlock sprigs, and the Articles of Confederation mean Shays’; Pittsburgh, stills, Hamilton’s excise tax, and Washington’s militia army mean Whiskey; John Fries and a tax on houses mean Fries’s Rebellion (1799).
trap.line: Real answer line: Shays’ Rebellion (or Shays’s Rebellion; prompt on Shays; do not accept “Whiskey Rebellion”)

topics.name: Sitting Bull
topics.kicker: Hunkpapa Lakota holy man and leader · Led resistance on the northern Plains
topics.briefing: Sitting Bull was a Hunkpapa Lakota holy man and leader who refused to give up his people’s land on the northern Plains. Weeks before the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876, he had a vision of soldiers falling into the Lakota camp, and the Lakota and Cheyenne then defeated George Armstrong Custer’s 7th Cavalry. He later spent four years in Canada, toured with Buffalo Bill’s Wild West, and was killed in 1890 when Indian police tried to arrest him at Standing Rock.

tossups.p: During a Sun Dance in June 1876, this holy man had a vision of soldiers falling upside down into his people’s camp like grasshoppers, a sign of a coming victory. Days later, Lakota and Cheyenne warriors led by Crazy Horse fought General George Crook’s army to a standstill at the Rosebud.
tossups.r: Later that month, this man’s followers helped defeat George Armstrong Custer at the Little Bighorn. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader.

tossups.p: In July 1881, this man surrendered at Fort Buford in Dakota Territory, where his young son Crow Foot handed over his father’s rifle. He had returned from four years in Canada after hunger and the disappearance of the buffalo left his followers struggling to survive.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader whose people had defeated George Custer at the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: In 1885, the Montreal studio of photographer William Notman took a portrait of this man standing beside a famous showman, later captioned “Foes in ’76, Friends in ’85.” That summer, this man toured for about four months with the showman’s traveling company.
tossups.r: That showman was Buffalo Bill Cody. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader who nicknamed Annie Oakley “Little Sure Shot.”

tossups.p: Lieutenant Bull Head and Sergeant Red Tomahawk led a group of Indian agency police to this man’s cabin on the Grand River before dawn one December morning. Agent James McLaughlin had sent them because he feared this man would lead a new religious movement among his people.
tossups.r: This man was killed during that arrest attempt on December 15, 1890. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader.

tossups.p: As a boy, this man was nicknamed “Slow” because he was so careful and deliberate. At about age 14, he counted coup on a Crow warrior, and his proud father then gave his own name to his son.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota holy man who led his people at the time of the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: Unlike Red Cloud, this leader refused to sign the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie, and he kept his followers off the reservations, hunting buffalo on the northern Plains. After gold was found in the Black Hills, the U.S. ordered all Lakota bands onto reservations by January 31, 1876.
tossups.r: This man’s refusal led to the war in which Custer was defeated. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader.

tossups.p: After seeing her shoot in St. Paul, Minnesota, in 1884, this man adopted a young sharpshooter from Ohio as an honorary daughter and gave her a Lakota name. The next year, both of them performed with the same traveling show.
tossups.r: That sharpshooter, Annie Oakley, became known by his nickname for her, “Little Sure Shot.” For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader.

tossups.p: After his surrender, this man was held as a prisoner of war at Fort Randall for nearly two years. In 1883, he was allowed to rejoin his people at an agency along the Missouri River, and he settled on a farm near the Grand River.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader who had fled to Canada after the Battle of the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: In 1864, this man fought against General Alfred Sully’s army at the Battle of Killdeer Mountain in Dakota Territory. He went on to become the most important leader of the Lakota bands that refused to live on reservations.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader who led the great camp at the Little Bighorn in 1876.

tossups.p: In 1889, this man tried to stop his people from signing an agreement that broke the Great Sioux Reservation into six smaller reservations and opened millions of acres to white settlers. Most Lakota men signed anyway, after long pressure from a commission led by General George Crook.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader who toured with Buffalo Bill’s Wild West in 1885.

tossups.p: The Lakota call a famous battle fought beside this man’s camp “the Greasy Grass,” after their name for the river there. His huge camp beside that river in Montana Territory included Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho people.
tossups.r: Americans call that 1876 battle the Little Bighorn, where Custer died. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota holy man.

tossups.p: This man and his followers called Canada the “Grandmother’s Land,” after Queen Victoria, and there he befriended James Walsh, an officer of the North-West Mounted Police, near Wood Mountain. Canada’s government refused to give his people a reservation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader who fled north after the Battle of the Little Bighorn.

tossups.p: In 1890, this man allowed Kicking Bear to teach a new religious movement at his camp, though historians still debate how strongly he believed in it. That movement had begun with the Paiute prophet Wovoka [“woh-VOH-kuh”].
tossups.r: Officials feared his role in that movement, the Ghost Dance, and sent police to arrest him. For 10 points, name this Lakota leader killed in December 1890.

tossups.p: At the start of a June 1876 battle, Major Marcus Reno’s soldiers charged the camp circle of this man’s own band at the southern end of the village, but warriors including Gall drove them back across the river and onto the bluffs.
tossups.r: Later that day, Lakota and Cheyenne warriors defeated George Armstrong Custer. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa holy man whose vision foretold that victory.

tossups.p: In 1953, some of this man’s relatives moved what they said were his remains from Fort Yates, North Dakota, to a hill near Mobridge, South Dakota. A granite bust of him there was carved by Korczak Ziolkowski [“KOR-chak jool-KOFF-skee”], the sculptor of the Crazy Horse Memorial.
tossups.r: He had been killed in 1890 during an attempt to arrest him. For 10 points, name this Hunkpapa Lakota leader, who toured with Buffalo Bill in 1885.

trap.title: Which Lakota leader?
trap.body: Several famous Lakota leaders appear in the same tossups. Sitting Bull was a Hunkpapa holy man whose vision foretold the victory at the Little Bighorn; Crazy Horse was an Oglala war leader who led warriors in the fighting there; and Red Cloud was an Oglala chief who signed the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie. Geronimo (Apache) and Chief Joseph (Nez Perce) led resistance in other regions.
trap.fix: Canada, Fort Buford, Buffalo Bill’s Wild West, “Little Sure Shot,” and the arrest at Standing Rock in 1890 mean Sitting Bull. The Rosebud, a surrender at Camp Robinson in 1877, and the unfinished mountain carving in South Dakota mean Crazy Horse.

topics.name: Slave rebellions
topics.kicker: Enslaved people taking up arms for freedom · Stono, Vesey, Nat Turner
topics.briefing: Enslaved people resisted slavery in many ways, and sometimes they took up arms. In 1739, men near South Carolina’s Stono River marched toward Spanish Florida, which promised them freedom, and in 1831 the preacher Nat Turner led a revolt in Virginia that terrified slaveholders, who answered with harsher laws. The most successful began in 1791 in Haiti, where formerly enslaved people won their independence in 1804.
topics.answerHtml: slave rebellions (or slave revolts, slave uprisings, or slave insurrections; prompt on rebellions or revolts alone)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Many of the men who took part in one of these events are thought to have come from the Kingdom of Kongo in Central Africa, and their leader was a man named Jemmy. In 1739, they seized guns from a store and marched south, beating drums and calling out “Liberty!”
tossups.r: That event began near the Stono River in South Carolina. For 10 points, name these events in which enslaved people took up arms for their freedom.

tossups.p: South Carolina’s Negro Act of 1740, which banned enslaved people from gathering in groups and made it illegal to teach them to write, was a response to one of these events. People in that event were heading for Spanish Florida, where the town of Fort Mose [“MOH-say”] near St. Augustine sheltered people who had escaped slavery in the Carolinas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these events, like the one near the Stono River in 1739, in which enslaved people fought for their freedom.

tossups.p: One of these events was to be fought under a banner reading “Death or Liberty,” but on the planned night in August 1800, a huge storm washed out roads and bridges near Richmond. Two men revealed the plan to their enslaver, and Governor James Monroe called out the militia.
tossups.r: Its leader was a blacksmith named Gabriel. For 10 points, name these events, such as Nat Turner’s in 1831, in which enslaved people took up arms.

tossups.p: After a plan to capture Richmond fell apart, the leader of one of these events escaped on a ship sailing down the James River, but he was turned in and captured at Norfolk. That leader, a blacksmith enslaved on Thomas Prosser’s plantation, was executed along with about 25 of his followers in 1800.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these events, also including Denmark Vesey’s planned one and Nat Turner’s, in which enslaved people fought for freedom.

tossups.p: In January 1811, Charles Deslondes [“day-LOHND”] led hundreds of people down the Mississippi River toward New Orleans in the largest of these events in U.S. history. Militia and U.S. Army troops stopped the marchers on a stretch of plantations called the German Coast, in the Territory of Orleans.
tossups.r: That territory became the state of Louisiana the next year. For 10 points, name these events, such as Nat Turner’s in Virginia, in which enslaved people took up arms.

tossups.p: A man who won 1,500 dollars in a city lottery used part of it to buy his freedom, then worked for years as a carpenter in Charleston before planning one of these events. He hoped his followers could later sail to Haiti, but informers revealed the plan in 1822 before it began.
tossups.r: That man was Denmark Vesey. For 10 points, name these events, such as Nat Turner’s in 1831, in which enslaved people fought for their freedom.

tossups.p: After one of these events was uncovered in 1822, Charleston’s African Methodist Episcopal church was destroyed, and South Carolina began jailing free Black sailors whenever their ships were in port. That church’s congregation later rebuilt as Emanuel AME, known as “Mother Emanuel.”
tossups.r: Denmark Vesey had planned that event. For 10 points, name these events in which enslaved people took up arms, including Nat Turner’s in Virginia.

tossups.p: Lawyer Thomas R. Gray interviewed the leader of one of these events in jail and published the leader’s “confessions” as a pamphlet in 1831. In 1968, William Styron won a Pulitzer Prize for a novel that retold the same story in the leader’s own voice.
tossups.r: That leader was Nat Turner. For 10 points, name these events, also including Denmark Vesey’s planned one in Charleston, in which enslaved people took up arms.

tossups.p: A solar eclipse in February 1831 convinced a preacher that God was signaling him to prepare for one of these events. After it was put down, that preacher hid for about two months before he was captured, tried, and executed.
tossups.r: The event took place in Southampton County, Virginia. For 10 points, name these events, such as the one led by Nat Turner, in which enslaved people fought for their freedom.

tossups.p: In 1832, Virginia’s legislature debated a plan to slowly end slavery in the state after one of these events, but it chose harsher laws instead, including new limits on Black preachers and church meetings. Southern leaders blamed William Lloyd Garrison’s new newspaper, _The Liberator_, for stirring up such events.
tossups.r: That 1831 event was led by Nat Turner. For 10 points, name these events in which enslaved people took up arms against their enslavers.

tossups.p: Yale professor Josiah Gibbs found an interpreter for the people involved in one of these events by walking New York’s docks and counting aloud in their Mende language. Those people had taken control of a Spanish schooner off Cuba in 1839 and were captured off Long Island.
tossups.r: John Quincy Adams helped win their freedom. For 10 points, name these events, such as the one aboard the _Amistad_, in which enslaved people fought for freedom.

tossups.p: Justice Joseph Story wrote an 1841 Supreme Court decision that freed the survivors of one of these events, and late that year they sailed home to Sierra Leone. Their leader, Sengbe Pieh, was known in the United States as Joseph Cinqué [“sin-KAY”].
tossups.r: Their ship was the _Amistad_. For 10 points, name these events, also including Nat Turner’s, in which enslaved people took up arms for their freedom.

tossups.p: In 1841, Madison Washington led one of these events aboard the _Creole_, a ship carrying people from Virginia to be sold in New Orleans. The ship then sailed to Nassau in the British Bahamas, where most of the people aboard were freed because Britain had ended slavery in its colonies.
tossups.r: Frederick Douglass later wrote a novella about Madison Washington. For 10 points, name these events, such as the one on the _Amistad_, in which enslaved people seized their freedom.

tossups.p: One of these events began in the French colony of Saint-Domingue [“san doh-MANG”] in 1791 and frightened enslavers in the United States for decades. Napoleon’s failure to win back that colony led him to sell Louisiana, and after Toussaint Louverture [“too-SAN loo-vair-TOOR”] died in a French prison, Jean-Jacques Dessalines [“deh-sah-LEEN”] declared independence in 1804.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these events in which enslaved people took up arms, one of which created the nation of Haiti.

tossups.p: In 1843, Henry Highland Garnet told a convention in Buffalo, “Let your motto be resistance!” Years earlier, David Walker’s _Appeal_ had urged enslaved Americans to fight back, and in 1859 John Brown hoped his raid on Harpers Ferry would spark a huge one of these events.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these events, such as Gabriel’s planned one in 1800 and Nat Turner’s in 1831, in which enslaved people took up arms for their freedom.

trap.title: The kind, not one
trap.body: Tossups on this answer line march through famous examples (Stono, Gabriel, Denmark Vesey, Nat Turner, the _Amistad_), but they ask for the whole category: “these events.” Answering with one example, like “Nat Turner’s Rebellion,” or with a related answer line, like the Haitian Revolution, John Brown’s raid, or the Underground Railroad, loses the tossup. Saying just “rebellion” or “revolt” earns a prompt.
trap.fix: When you hear “these events” or “this kind of event,” say “slave rebellions” (or “slave revolts”). Save the leaders’ names for questions that ask for “this man,” like Nat Turner, Denmark Vesey, or Gabriel.
trap.line: Real answer line: slave rebellions (or slave revolts; accept slave uprisings or slave insurrections; prompt on rebellions or revolts alone)

topics.name: Stephen A. Douglas
topics.kicker: The “Little Giant” of Illinois · Debated Abraham Lincoln in 1858
topics.briefing: Stephen A. Douglas was a short man, but his booming voice and fierce debating earned him the nickname “the Little Giant.” The Illinois senator wrote the Kansas–Nebraska Act, which let settlers vote on slavery, and in 1858 he kept his Senate seat after seven famous debates with Abraham Lincoln. Two years later, Lincoln beat him for the presidency.
topics.answerHtml: Stephen A. Douglas (or Stephen Arnold Douglas; prompt on “Little Giant”; do not accept “Frederick Douglass”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: One opponent mocked this man’s argument as being as thin as soup made by boiling “the shadow of a pigeon that had starved to death.” At Freeport, this man had claimed that settlers could still keep slavery out of a territory by refusing to pass laws to protect it, despite the _Dred Scott_ decision.
tossups.r: That opponent was Abraham Lincoln, who debated this man seven times in 1858. For 10 points, name this Illinois senator nicknamed the “Little Giant.”

tossups.p: This senator broke with President James Buchanan in 1857 by opposing the Lecompton [“leh-KOMP-tun”] Constitution for Kansas, saying it had not been fairly approved by the territory’s voters. He insisted that he did not care whether slavery was “voted down or voted up.”
tossups.r: Years earlier, he wrote the Kansas–Nebraska Act. For 10 points, name this Illinois Democrat who debated Abraham Lincoln in 1858.

tossups.p: Hoping that a transcontinental railroad would run west from Chicago, this senator pushed to organize the land west of Iowa and Missouri. His 1854 bill to do that repealed the Missouri Compromise’s ban on slavery north of the 36°30′ line.
tossups.r: That law, the Kansas–Nebraska Act, let settlers decide on slavery by popular sovereignty. For 10 points, name this “Little Giant” from Illinois.

tossups.p: This politician once joked that he could travel from Boston to Chicago by the light of his own burning effigies, after a law he wrote angered many Northerners. Opponents of that law soon founded the Republican Party, and fighting broke out in “Bleeding Kansas.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this author of the Kansas–Nebraska Act, an Illinois senator who debated Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: After Henry Clay’s “Omnibus Bill” fell apart in the summer of 1850, this senator split it into separate bills and steered each one through Congress. Those laws admitted California as a free state and created a tougher Fugitive Slave Act.
tossups.r: Four years later, he wrote the Kansas–Nebraska Act. For 10 points, name this Illinois Democrat called the “Little Giant.”

tossups.p: Born in Brandon, Vermont, in 1813, this man moved to Illinois as a young man and served on the Illinois Supreme Court, which is why one rival kept calling him “Judge.” He later served in the U.S. House and then in the Senate from 1847 until his death.
tossups.r: That rival was Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this “Little Giant” who beat Lincoln in an 1858 Senate race.

tossups.p: In one presidential election, this candidate finished second in the popular vote but won the electoral votes of only Missouri and part of New Jersey. Breaking with custom, he gave campaign speeches across the country, even traveling into the South to urge voters to stay loyal to the Union.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Northern Democratic nominee who lost the 1860 election to his old debate opponent, Abraham Lincoln.

tossups.p: After his party’s 1860 convention in Charleston, South Carolina, broke apart, this man was nominated at a second convention in Baltimore, with Georgia’s Herschel Johnson as his running mate. Southern Democrats who walked out chose John C. Breckinridge instead.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Northern Democratic candidate in 1860, the “Little Giant” who had debated Abraham Lincoln two years earlier.

tossups.p: Weeks before he died of typhoid fever in June 1861, this man declared that “there can be no neutrals in this war, only patriots—or traitors.” He spent his last months urging Northern Democrats to support the Union and the new president who had beaten him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Illinois senator who lost the 1860 election to Abraham Lincoln, two years after their famous debates.

tossups.p: According to a famous story, this man held Abraham Lincoln’s hat while Lincoln gave his first inaugural address in March 1861. After the attack on Fort Sumter, this Democrat urged his party’s members in the North to back the war to save the Union.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Illinois senator, Lincoln’s longtime rival, who was nicknamed the “Little Giant.”

tossups.p: This man’s 1858 campaign included seven three-hour joint appearances with his opponent, beginning at Ottawa and ending at Alton. Because senators were then chosen by state legislatures, the newly elected Illinois legislature decided the race and gave this man another term.
tossups.r: His opponent in those debates was Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this Illinois senator, the “Little Giant.”

tossups.p: This man lost the Democratic presidential nomination to Franklin Pierce in 1852 and to James Buchanan in 1856. For years he chaired the Senate Committee on Territories, where he wrote bills to organize new lands in the West.
tossups.r: One of those bills became the Kansas–Nebraska Act. For 10 points, name this Illinois senator who debated Abraham Lincoln in 1858.

tossups.p: This man’s second wife, Adele Cutts, was a grandniece of Dolley Madison. In the 1850s, this man championed the idea that the settlers in each new territory should vote on whether to allow slavery there.
tossups.r: That idea was called popular sovereignty. For 10 points, name this Illinois senator who debated Abraham Lincoln in 1858.

tossups.p: In a famous 1858 speech, an opponent suggested that this man had worked with Franklin Pierce, Roger Taney [“TAW-nee”], and James Buchanan to spread slavery, calling the four men by their first names. That speech warned that “a house divided against itself cannot stand.”
tossups.r: That opponent was Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this Illinois senator, the “Little Giant,” whom Lincoln debated later that year.

tossups.p: In an 1854 speech at Peoria, Abraham Lincoln attacked a law written by this man, arguing that slavery should not spread into new territories. That law, which this man pushed through Congress, led to violence between proslavery and antislavery settlers.
tossups.r: That law was the Kansas–Nebraska Act. For 10 points, name this Illinois senator nicknamed the “Little Giant.”

trap.title: One S or two?
trap.body: Stephen A. Douglas and Frederick Douglass have names that sound exactly alike, and both turn up in questions about the 1850s. Douglas (one s) was the Illinois senator who debated Abraham Lincoln; Douglass (two s’s) escaped slavery and became a famous abolitionist speaker, writer, and newspaper editor. Real answer lines say “do not accept Frederick Douglass,” and this site checks the spelling, too.
trap.fix: The Senate, the Kansas–Nebraska Act, popular sovereignty, Freeport, and the 1858 debates mean Stephen Douglas. Escaping slavery, his _Narrative_, and _The North Star_ mean Frederick Douglass. Type “Stephen Douglas,” with one s, to be safe.

topics.name: The Federalist Papers
topics.kicker: 85 essays signed “Publius” · Urged New York to ratify the Constitution
topics.briefing: To persuade New Yorkers to ratify the new Constitution, Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay wrote 85 essays in 1787 and 1788, all signed with the pen name “Publius.” Hamilton wrote 51, Madison 29, and Jay 5. Essays like No. 10, on the dangers of factions, and No. 51, which says “if men were angels, no government would be necessary,” are still quoted by Supreme Court justices.
topics.answerHtml: The Federalist Papers (or The Federalist; prompt on one numbered essay, such as Federalist No. 10; do not accept “Anti-Federalist Papers” or “Federalist Party”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the 1960s, statisticians Frederick Mosteller and David Wallace counted how often words like “upon” and “whilst” appeared in these works to figure out who wrote twelve of them whose authorship was disputed.
tossups.r: Their counts pointed to James Madison rather than Alexander Hamilton. For 10 points, name these 85 essays, all signed “Publius,” that defended the U.S. Constitution.

tossups.p: Montesquieu [“MON-tes-kyoo”] is called “the oracle” on the separation of powers in one of these essays. A later one argues that “ambition must be made to counteract ambition” and that “if men were angels, no government would be necessary.”
tossups.r: James Madison wrote both of those essays, Nos. 47 and 51. For 10 points, name this series of essays that urged New Yorkers to ratify the Constitution.

tossups.p: One of these essays claims that “the most common and durable source” of political divisions “has been the various and unequal distribution of property.” That essay argues that a large republic is the best way to control the dangers of “faction.”
tossups.r: That essay, No. 10, was written by James Madison. For 10 points, name this series of 85 essays published under the pen name “Publius.”

tossups.p: Courts have “neither force nor will, but merely judgment,” according to one of these essays, which calls them “the least dangerous” branch. That essay, No. 78, also defends letting judges serve during “good behaviour” and supports the idea later called judicial review.
tossups.r: Its author, Alexander Hamilton, wrote 51 of these essays. For 10 points, name this series written to defend the new Constitution.

tossups.p: “Energy in the executive is a leading character in the definition of good government,” declares one of these essays, which argues for a single president instead of a council. Another, No. 68, defends the system of electors that chooses the president.
tossups.r: Alexander Hamilton wrote both. For 10 points, name this series of essays by Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay.

tossups.p: In one of these essays, the author argued that a bill of rights was unnecessary and might even be dangerous, because it would seem to limit powers the new government had never been given. That essay, No. 84, was one of the last in the series.
tossups.r: Its author, Alexander Hamilton, wrote most of these essays. For 10 points, name these 85 essays that defended the Constitution in 1787 and 1788.

tossups.p: The pen name on these essays honored a Roman leader who helped found the Roman Republic after its last king was overthrown. Three different men wrote these essays, but every one of them was signed with that single name.
tossups.r: That name was “Publius.” For 10 points, name these essays by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay.

tossups.p: The first of these essays appeared in New York’s _Independent Journal_ on October 27, 1787, and others soon ran in the _New-York Packet_ and the _Daily Advertiser_. Each essay was addressed “To the People of the State of New York.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this series of essays signed “Publius,” which urged New Yorkers to ratify the Constitution.

tossups.p: In 1788, the New York printers John and Archibald McLean collected these essays into a two-volume book, including some that had not yet appeared in any newspaper. That book’s title described the essays as a collection written “in favour of the new Constitution.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this series of 85 essays by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay.

tossups.p: One author of these essays wrote No. 64, which defends giving the president and the Senate the power to make treaties. That same author argued in No. 2 that Providence had given “this one connected country to one united people.”
tossups.r: That author, John Jay, wrote only five of these essays. For 10 points, name this series, mostly written by Alexander Hamilton and James Madison.

tossups.p: In a song that closes the first act of a 2015 Broadway musical, Aaron Burr counts how many of these essays each writer produced: five, twenty-nine, and fifty-one. That song, “Non-Stop,” marvels that the title character writes “like you’re running out of time.”
tossups.r: That musical is _Hamilton_. For 10 points, name this series of essays signed “Publius” that defended the Constitution.

tossups.p: The first of these essays asks whether societies can set up good government “from reflection and choice,” or whether they must always depend on “accident and force.” Its author went on to write 51 of the 85 essays in the series.
tossups.r: That author was Alexander Hamilton. For 10 points, name this series of essays that urged the people of New York to ratify the Constitution.

tossups.p: Opponents of the Constitution made their case in essays of their own, written under pen names such as “Brutus” and “Cato.” These essays were aimed at New York, which ratified the Constitution by a vote of 30 to 27 at Poughkeepsie [“puh-KIP-see”] in July 1788.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these 85 essays by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay.

tossups.p: A promise that the national government’s powers would be “few and defined,” while those left to the states would be “numerous and indefinite,” appears in one of these essays. That essay, No. 45, came from the same author as the famous essays on factions and on angels.
tossups.r: That author was James Madison. For 10 points, name this series of essays defending the Constitution, all signed “Publius.”

tossups.p: Shortly before his fatal duel in 1804, one writer left a friend a list of which of these essays he had written. That list claimed some essays that his co-author, the future fourth president, later said were his own.
tossups.r: That writer was Alexander Hamilton. For 10 points, name this series of 85 essays that defended the Constitution.

trap.title: Essays, not the party
trap.body: “Federalist” is part of several answer lines. _The Federalist Papers_ are the 85 essays of 1787–1788; the Federalist Party was the party of Alexander Hamilton and John Adams in the 1790s; and the Anti-Federalists were the Constitution’s opponents, who wrote essays of their own under names like “Brutus.” Saying the party, “Federalists,” or “Anti-Federalist Papers” loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “these essays,” “this series,” or numbered essays like No. 10 and No. 51 mean _The Federalist Papers_, and plain “The Federalist” is fine too. “This party,” with John Adams or the Alien and Sedition Acts, means the Federalist Party.
trap.line: Real answer line: The Federalist Papers (or The Federalist; do not accept “Anti-Federalist Papers” or “Federalist Party”)

topics.name: Thurgood Marshall
topics.kicker: First African American Supreme Court justice · Led the NAACP’s legal fight
topics.briefing: As the NAACP’s top lawyer, Thurgood Marshall traveled the country fighting segregation in court, and in 1954 he won _Brown v. Board of Education_, which struck down segregated public schools. In 1967, President Lyndon Johnson made him the first African American justice on the Supreme Court, where he served for 24 years. The main airport serving his hometown, Baltimore, is named for him.
topics.answerHtml: Thurgood Marshall (prompt on Thurgood alone; do not accept “John Marshall” or “George Marshall”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This lawyer and his mentor won a 1936 case, _Murray v. Pearson_, that forced the University of Maryland’s law school to admit a Black student. That school’s segregation policy had kept this man from studying there, so he earned his law degree at Howard University instead.
tossups.r: He later argued _Brown v. Board of Education_. For 10 points, name this lawyer who became the first African American Supreme Court justice.

tossups.p: This lawyer helped a Houston dentist, Lonnie Smith, win a 1944 Supreme Court case that struck down Texas’s all-white Democratic primary elections. Two years later, he won _Morgan v. Virginia_, which struck down a state law segregating passengers on buses that crossed state lines.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this NAACP lawyer who argued _Brown v. Board of Education_ and later became the first African American Supreme Court justice.

tossups.p: Texas set up a separate law school for Black students to keep Heman Sweatt out of the University of Texas, but this lawyer convinced the Supreme Court in 1950 that it was not equal. The law school at Houston’s Texas Southern University was later named for this man.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this NAACP lawyer who argued _Brown v. Board of Education_ and became the first Black Supreme Court justice.

tossups.p: In 1965, this man became the first African American to serve as Solicitor General, the lawyer who argues cases for the federal government before the Supreme Court. Four years earlier, John F. Kennedy had named him to a federal appeals court in New York.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this man whom Lyndon Johnson appointed in 1967 as the first Black justice on the Supreme Court.

tossups.p: In a 1987 speech marking the Constitution’s 200th anniversary, this justice said the government the framers designed was “defective from the start” because it accepted slavery. He retired from the Court in 1991 and was replaced by Clarence Thomas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this justice who had argued _Brown v. Board of Education_ and became the first African American on the Supreme Court.

tossups.p: In _Furman v. Georgia_ (1972), this justice wrote that the death penalty always violates the Eighth Amendment’s ban on “cruel and unusual punishments.” He and William Brennan often wrote dissents together in his later years on the Court.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this first African American Supreme Court justice, who had argued _Brown v. Board of Education_ as a lawyer.

tossups.p: This man was born “Thoroughgood” in Baltimore in 1908 but shortened his first name in second grade. As a boy, he later recalled, he was punished for misbehaving at school by having to memorize parts of the U.S. Constitution.
tossups.r: He later led the NAACP’s legal fight against segregation. For 10 points, name this first African American Supreme Court justice.

tossups.p: This lawyer, nicknamed “Mr. Civil Rights,” founded the NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund in 1940 and led it for more than twenty years. His team traveled across the South to challenge segregated schools, buses, and voting rules in court.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lawyer who argued _Brown v. Board of Education_ and became a Supreme Court justice in 1967.

tossups.p: The Senate confirmed this man to his most famous job by a vote of 69 to 11 in 1967, after Tom C. Clark retired because his son had become attorney general. Earlier, this man had argued the government’s cases as Solicitor General.
tossups.r: He was appointed by Lyndon Johnson. For 10 points, name this first African American Supreme Court justice.

tossups.p: In 2005, the main airport serving Baltimore was renamed in honor of this man, who grew up in that city. A 2017 film named for him starred Chadwick Boseman and showed him defending a man in a Connecticut trial early in his career.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this NAACP lawyer who argued _Brown v. Board of Education_ and became the first Black Supreme Court justice.

tossups.p: In the 1958 case _Cooper v. Aaron_, this lawyer argued that Arkansas officials could not delay the integration of Little Rock’s Central High School, and all nine justices signed an opinion agreeing with him.
tossups.r: Four years earlier, he had won _Brown v. Board of Education_. For 10 points, name this lawyer who became the first African American Supreme Court justice.

tossups.p: To show that segregation harmed children, this lawyer’s team presented psychologists Kenneth and Mamie Clark’s studies in which many Black children preferred white dolls. In that case, this lawyer faced John W. Davis, a former presidential nominee who argued for South Carolina.
tossups.r: That case was _Brown v. Board of Education_. For 10 points, name this NAACP lawyer who later became the first African American Supreme Court justice.

tossups.p: This man graduated in 1930 from Lincoln University in Pennsylvania, then finished first in his class at Howard University’s law school, where he studied under Charles Hamilton Houston. He joined Houston on the NAACP’s legal staff in the 1930s.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lawyer who argued _Brown v. Board of Education_ and became the first Black Supreme Court justice.

tossups.p: In _McLaurin v. Oklahoma State Regents_, this lawyer’s NAACP team challenged rules that made a Black graduate student sit apart from his classmates, even in the cafeteria and library. The Supreme Court ruled for that student in 1950, on the same day as a Texas law school case.
tossups.r: Four years later, this lawyer won _Brown v. Board of Education_. For 10 points, name this first African American Supreme Court justice.

tossups.p: When this man died in 1993, his body lay in repose in the Great Hall of the Supreme Court building, and thousands of mourners filed past. Two years earlier, he had retired after 24 years on the Court.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this justice appointed by Lyndon Johnson, the first African American on the Supreme Court.

trap.title: Which Marshall?
trap.body: Three famous Marshalls show up in American history questions. Thurgood Marshall argued _Brown v. Board of Education_ and became the first African American Supreme Court justice in 1967; John Marshall was the fourth Chief Justice (1801–1835), who wrote _Marbury v. Madison_; and George C. Marshall was the World War II general behind the Marshall Plan. Real answer lines say “do not accept John Marshall.”
trap.fix: Thurgood clues: the NAACP, _Brown v. Board_, Howard University, Charles Hamilton Houston, Solicitor General, and Lyndon Johnson. John Marshall clues: judicial review, _Marbury v. Madison_, and the early 1800s. “Marshall” alone is fine, but say “Thurgood” if you have time.
trap.line: Real answer line: Thurgood Marshall (do not accept “John Marshall”)

topics.name: Veto
topics.kicker: The president’s power to reject a bill · Two-thirds of Congress can override it
topics.briefing: When Congress passes a bill, the president can sign it into law or send it back with a veto, from the Latin for “I forbid.” Congress can still pass the bill over the president’s objection, but only with a two-thirds vote in both the House and the Senate, which rarely happens. Franklin Roosevelt holds the record, with 635 vetoes.
topics.answerHtml: veto (accept word forms like vetoes; accept specific kinds like the pocket veto or line-item veto; do not accept “override”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This word comes from the Latin for “I forbid,” which tribunes in ancient Rome could say to block the actions of other officials. Article I, Section 7 of the U.S. Constitution describes how this action works and how Congress can respond to it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this power of the president to reject a bill, which Congress can override with a two-thirds vote in each house.

tossups.p: George Washington first used this power in 1792 against a bill dividing up seats in the House of Representatives, and he used it only one other time. His successors John Adams and Thomas Jefferson never used it at all.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this power that lets a president reject a bill passed by Congress.

tossups.p: Every member of John Tyler’s cabinet except Daniel Webster resigned in 1841 after Tyler used this power against bills creating a new national bank. In 1845, Tyler also became the first president to have Congress overturn one of these actions, on a bill about ships called revenue cutters.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this presidential power to reject a bill, which Congress can override by a two-thirds vote.

tossups.p: Opponents mocked one president as “King Andrew the First” because he used this power more often than all the presidents before him combined. Two of his most famous uses of it blocked money for the Maysville Road and a new charter for the Second Bank of the United States.
tossups.r: That president was Andrew Jackson. For 10 points, name this power of the president to reject bills passed by Congress.

tossups.p: Andrew Johnson used this power against the Civil Rights Act of 1866, but Congress passed it anyway, making it the first major law ever passed over a president’s objection. Congress overturned fifteen of Johnson’s uses of this power, a record, including those on the Reconstruction Acts of 1867.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this presidential power to reject bills, which Congress can override with a two-thirds vote.

tossups.p: Franklin Roosevelt holds the record for using this power, with 635 uses in just over twelve years. The president in second place, Grover Cleveland, used it more than 400 times in his first term alone, often against private pension bills for Civil War veterans.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this power that lets a president reject a bill passed by Congress.

tossups.p: As mayor of Buffalo, one future president earned a nickname for using this power to block wasteful spending. As president, he used it on a bill to give ten thousand dollars’ worth of seed to drought-stricken Texas farmers, writing that “the Government should not support the people.”
tossups.r: That man was Grover Cleveland. For 10 points, name this presidential power to reject a bill.

tossups.p: If Congress adjourns within ten days, not counting Sundays, after sending a bill to the president, he can kill it just by not signing it, a move known as the “pocket” form of this action. Abraham Lincoln used that form against the Wade-Davis Bill in 1864.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this presidential power to reject bills, which Congress can usually override with two-thirds of each house.

tossups.p: A 1996 law let the president cancel individual spending items in a bill after signing it, but the Supreme Court struck that law down in _Clinton v. City of New York_. Most state governors have that “line-item” version of this power, and so did the president of the Confederacy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this power of an executive to reject a bill, which Congress can override with a two-thirds vote.

tossups.p: Harry Truman used this power against the Taft–Hartley Act, which limited labor unions, but the act became law anyway in 1947. In 1973, Richard Nixon’s use of it also failed to stop the War Powers Resolution, which limits how long troops can fight without approval from Congress.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this presidential power to reject bills, which can be overridden by two-thirds of each house of Congress.

tossups.p: Ronald Reagan used this power against a 1986 law placing economic sanctions on South Africa over apartheid, but Congress passed the law anyway. Back in 1919, Woodrow Wilson’s use of it failed to stop the Volstead Act, which enforced Prohibition.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this power of the president to reject a bill passed by Congress.

tossups.p: The five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, including the United States, can each block a resolution by using this power. At home, a president who uses it must return the bill with written objections to the house of Congress where it began.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this power to reject a proposed law, which Congress can override with a two-thirds vote.

tossups.p: Just before leaving office in 1817, James Madison used this power against John C. Calhoun’s Bonus Bill for roads and canals, saying the Constitution did not allow it. Five years later, James Monroe used it to stop a bill collecting tolls on the Cumberland Road.
tossups.r: Such projects were called internal improvements. For 10 points, name this presidential power to reject a bill passed by Congress.

tossups.p: Chester Arthur used this power against a bill banning Chinese laborers for twenty years, then signed a ten-year version. Later that year, the Rivers and Harbors Act of 1882 became law even though Arthur had used this power against it as wasteful spending.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this power of the president to reject a bill, which can be overridden by two-thirds of Congress.

tossups.p: To reverse this action, the House needs 290 votes if all 435 members vote, and the Senate needs 67 if all 100 senators vote. Because that takes such a large majority, Congress has reversed only a small share of these actions.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this power of the president to reject a bill passed by Congress.

trap.title: Power, override, or filibuster?
trap.body: Several lawmaking answers get mixed up. The veto is the president’s power to reject a bill; an override is how Congress fights back, with a two-thirds vote in each house; and a filibuster is a Senate tactic of endless debate. Answering “override” when the question asks for the president’s action, or “filibuster” for anything a president does, loses the tossup.
trap.fix: If a president (or a governor, or a UN Security Council member) blocks something, the answer is “veto,” and specific kinds like “pocket veto” and “line-item veto” count too. If Congress is pushing back with two-thirds of each house, the answer is “override.”
trap.line: Real answer line: veto (accept word forms like vetoes; accept specific kinds like pocket veto or line-item veto; do not accept “override”)

topics.name: Siege of Vicksburg
topics.kicker: Grant’s 1863 siege on the Mississippi · Split the Confederacy in two
topics.briefing: In 1863, Ulysses S. Grant’s army trapped nearly 30,000 Confederate soldiers inside Vicksburg, Mississippi, a fortress city on high bluffs above the Mississippi River. For 47 days, Union cannons and gunboats shelled the city, and many families lived in caves dug into the hillsides. When it surrendered on July 4, the day after the Battle of Gettysburg ended, the Union soon controlled the whole river and split the Confederacy in two.
topics.answerHtml: Siege of Vicksburg (or Vicksburg Campaign; prompt on “siege” alone; do not accept “Port Hudson”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: After this event, Abraham Lincoln wrote to Ulysses S. Grant admitting “you were right, and I was wrong” about Grant’s decision to turn inland instead of joining Nathaniel Banks. Before this event began, Grant’s army had crossed the river south of its target and won five battles in less than three weeks.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1863 Union victory in which Grant captured a Mississippi River city on July 4.

tossups.p: The ironclad USS _Cairo_ sank in the Yazoo River after hitting a mine during an early Union attempt to reach the target of this campaign. About a century later, the ship was raised and put on display at the national military park that honors this campaign.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1863 siege in which Ulysses S. Grant captured a Mississippi city on July 4.

tossups.p: Benjamin Grierson’s cavalry raid, the basis of the John Wayne film _The Horse Soldiers_, distracted Confederate defenders during this campaign. While Grierson rode south through Mississippi, the main Union army crossed the river at Bruinsburg in one of the largest amphibious landings in U.S. history before World War II.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1863 campaign in which Ulysses S. Grant besieged and captured a Mississippi River city.

tossups.p: During this siege, many residents dug caves into the city’s hillsides to escape constant shelling, and some ate mule meat as food ran out. After 47 days, the Confederate commander surrendered his army of nearly 30,000 men.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this siege that ended on July 4, 1863, giving the Union control of the Mississippi River.

tossups.p: On the night of April 16, 1863, David Dixon Porter’s gunboats ran past the batteries guarding the target of this campaign, taking heavy fire from the bluffs. Those boats then helped carry Union troops across the river south of the city.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this campaign that ended when John C. Pemberton surrendered to Ulysses S. Grant on July 4, 1863.

tossups.p: Ulysses S. Grant’s army captured the Mississippi state capital, Jackson, and then defeated John C. Pemberton’s army at Champion Hill and the Big Black River Bridge in May 1863. Pemberton’s troops then retreated into the city whose capture was the goal of this campaign.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this campaign and siege that ended with the city’s surrender on July 4, 1863.

tossups.p: During the winter before this siege, Union soldiers tried to dig a canal across a peninsula so boats could bypass the city’s guns, and they also tried routes through Lake Providence and the Yazoo Pass. All of those attempts failed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Mississippi River siege won by Ulysses S. Grant in July 1863.

tossups.p: William T. Sherman’s attack at Chickasaw Bayou failed in December 1862, the same month that Earl Van Dorn’s cavalry destroyed a Union supply base at Holly Springs. Those setbacks forced Ulysses S. Grant to find a new route to the city he was trying to capture.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1863 siege of a Confederate stronghold on the Mississippi River, which ended on July 4.

tossups.p: Union soldiers dug a tunnel under the 3rd Louisiana Redan and exploded a mine there on June 25, 1863, during this siege. Ulysses S. Grant had begun the siege after two direct assaults on the city’s defenses failed in May.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this siege that ended on July 4, 1863, a day after the Battle of Gettysburg.

tossups.p: The Confederate commander in this siege was a Pennsylvania-born general who had sided with the South, and he hoped in vain that Joseph E. Johnston’s army would come to rescue him. That general was John C. Pemberton.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this siege in which Pemberton surrendered a Mississippi River city to Ulysses S. Grant in 1863.

tossups.p: Rather than send them to prison camps, Ulysses S. Grant paroled nearly 30,000 Confederate soldiers who surrendered at the end of this siege. He had first demanded an unconditional surrender, just as he had at Fort Donelson the year before.
tossups.r: The surrender came on July 4, 1863, the day after the Battle of Gettysburg ended. For 10 points, name this siege of a Mississippi River city.

tossups.p: After this siege and the surrender of Port Hudson five days later, Abraham Lincoln wrote that “the Father of Waters again goes unvexed to the sea.” Union control of that river split the Confederacy and cut off Texas, Arkansas, and Louisiana.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1863 siege in which Ulysses S. Grant captured a key Confederate city on the Mississippi River.

tossups.p: During this siege, Ulysses S. Grant removed John McClernand from command after McClernand published an order praising his own troops and suggesting that other units had let them down in a failed assault. Grant’s other corps commanders there included William T. Sherman and James McPherson.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this siege that ended with John C. Pemberton’s surrender on July 4, 1863.

tossups.p: In 1862, after capturing New Orleans, David Farragut’s fleet demanded the surrender of the city targeted in this siege, but its defenders refused. Because the city’s guns controlled the river from high bluffs, people called it the “Gibraltar of the Confederacy.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1863 siege in which Ulysses S. Grant finally captured that city.

tossups.p: The city at the center of this siege stood on high bluffs above a hairpin bend in a river, so its cannons could fire on any boat passing below. Capturing it was a key step toward the goal of Winfield Scott’s Anaconda Plan.
tossups.r: That plan aimed to split the Confederacy in two. For 10 points, name this 1863 siege that ended with a Union victory on July 4.
