trap.title: Siege, river, or Gettysburg?
trap.body: Tossups on this siege are full of Mississippi River clues, but the river, the Anaconda Plan, and Port Hudson are separate answer lines. And because the city fell on July 4, 1863, the day after the Battle of Gettysburg ended, players sometimes blurt out “Gettysburg” when they hear July 1863. Ulysses S. Grant’s other Western victories, Fort Donelson, Shiloh, and Chattanooga, are traps too.
trap.fix: Pemberton, caves, Champion Hill, Grierson’s Raid, Porter’s gunboats, and a siege of 47 days mean Vicksburg. Robert E. Lee, Pickett’s Charge, and Pennsylvania mean Gettysburg. “Vicksburg” alone is enough.
trap.line: Real answer line: Siege of Vicksburg (or Vicksburg Campaign)

topics.name: WikiLeaks
topics.kicker: Website that publishes secret documents · Founded by Julian Assange in 2006
topics.briefing: The Australian Julian Assange founded WikiLeaks in 2006 to publish secret documents, often sent by anonymous sources. In 2010 it released hundreds of thousands of classified U.S. military reports and diplomatic messages provided by Chelsea Manning, then an Army intelligence analyst; supporters praised it for exposing government secrets, while U.S. officials said the releases put lives at risk. In 2024, Assange made a plea deal with U.S. prosecutors, was freed from a British prison, and returned home to Australia.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In June 2024, under a plea agreement, this organization’s founder pleaded guilty to one charge in a U.S. federal court on Saipan, in the Northern Mariana Islands, and was freed to fly home to Australia. He had spent the previous five years in London’s Belmarsh prison fighting extradition to the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this website, founded by Julian Assange, that publishes secret documents from anonymous sources.

tossups.p: As a teenage computer hacker in Melbourne, this organization’s founder used the online name “Mendax,” and he later pleaded guilty to hacking charges in Australia in the 1990s. That founder had been born in Townsville, Australia, in 1971.
tossups.r: He started this organization in 2006. For 10 points, name this website, founded by Julian Assange, that publishes secret documents.

tossups.p: In June 2012, this organization’s founder walked into Ecuador’s embassy in London to avoid being sent to Sweden for questioning in a criminal investigation that was later dropped. He lived inside the embassy for nearly seven years until Ecuador withdrew his asylum in 2019 and British police arrested him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this website founded by Julian Assange, which publishes secret government documents from anonymous sources.

tossups.p: In 2013, a military court convicted an Army intelligence analyst of giving this organization hundreds of thousands of classified files and sentenced her to 35 years in prison. President Barack Obama commuted that sentence in 2017, and she was released that May.
tossups.r: That analyst was Chelsea Manning. For 10 points, name this website founded by Julian Assange.

tossups.p: In July 2010, this organization worked with _The New York Times_, _The Guardian_, and _Der Spiegel_ to publish tens of thousands of secret U.S. military reports about the war in Afghanistan. Three months later, it released nearly 400,000 reports about the Iraq War.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this website, founded by Julian Assange, that publishes classified documents.

tossups.p: Beginning in November 2010, this organization and several newspapers published parts of about 250,000 messages sent between the U.S. State Department and American embassies around the world. The release embarrassed diplomats by revealing their private opinions of foreign leaders, and journalists nicknamed it “Cablegate.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this website founded by Julian Assange, which publishes secret government documents.

tossups.p: In December 2010, Visa, MasterCard, and PayPal stopped handling donations to this organization, and the hacker group Anonymous attacked those companies’ websites in response. Bank of America also cut off payments to this group that month.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this website whose founder, Julian Assange, had just begun releasing secret U.S. diplomatic cables.

tossups.p: In 2008, a U.S. federal judge briefly ordered this organization’s web address shut down after the Swiss bank Julius Baer [“BAIR”] sued over documents it had published, but the judge reversed that order about two weeks later.
tossups.r: Despite its name, this organization has no connection to Wikipedia. For 10 points, name this website founded by Julian Assange.

tossups.p: In 2017, this organization began publishing “Vault 7,” a large set of files describing hacking tools used by the CIA. Earlier, in 2011, it released secret U.S. military files on prisoners held at Guantánamo Bay.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this website, founded by Julian Assange, that publishes secret documents from anonymous sources.

tossups.p: During the 2016 U.S. presidential campaign, this organization published emails taken from the Democratic National Committee and from John Podesta, the chairman of Hillary Clinton’s campaign. In 2018, a U.S. special counsel charged twelve Russian military intelligence officers with stealing those emails.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this website founded by Julian Assange that publishes secret documents from anonymous sources.

tossups.p: In 2013, Sarah Harrison, a journalist working for this organization, traveled with Edward Snowden when he flew from Hong Kong to Moscow after revealing secret National Security Agency programs. Snowden had given his documents to journalists, not to this group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this website founded by Julian Assange that publishes secret documents.

tossups.p: Benedict Cumberbatch played this organization’s founder in the 2013 film _The Fifth Estate_. That same year, Alex Gibney released a documentary about this organization and its sources called _We Steal Secrets_.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this website, founded by Julian Assange in 2006, that publishes secret documents from anonymous sources.

tossups.p: In 2018, the Icelandic journalist Kristinn Hrafnsson became this organization’s editor-in-chief, replacing its founder. That same year, Ecuador cut off the founder’s internet access inside its embassy in London, where he had been living since 2012.
tossups.r: That founder was Julian Assange. For 10 points, name this website that publishes secret documents.

tossups.p: In 2019, the U.S. Justice Department charged this organization’s founder with 18 crimes, 17 of them under the Espionage Act of 1917. His supporters argued that the charges threatened press freedom, while prosecutors said his publications had put people’s lives at risk.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this website, founded by Julian Assange, that publishes secret documents from anonymous sources.

tossups.p: In May 2010, the former hacker Adrian Lamo reported an Army private serving in Iraq to investigators after she described, in online chats, sending classified files to this organization. That private, then known as Bradley Manning, was arrested within days.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this website founded by Julian Assange that publishes secret documents.

trap.title: Website, founder, or source?
trap.body: Tossups on this answer line are packed with people. Julian Assange founded it, and Chelsea Manning gave it hundreds of thousands of secret files. Edward Snowden, who revealed secret National Security Agency programs in 2013, is often mixed up with it, even though he gave his documents to journalists instead. Naming a person when the question asks for “this organization” or “this website” loses the tossup.
trap.fix: Listen for the noun: “this organization,” “this group,” or “this website” wants WikiLeaks; “this man” or “this Australian” wants Assange; “this analyst” or “this soldier” wants Manning. The Pentagon Papers (1971) were a different case, made public by Daniel Ellsberg.

topics.name: William Henry Seward
topics.kicker: Lincoln’s Secretary of State · Bought Alaska from Russia in 1867
topics.briefing: William Henry Seward was a New York governor and senator who expected to win the 1860 Republican nomination, but Abraham Lincoln beat him and then made him Secretary of State. On the night Lincoln was shot, Seward survived an attack in his own bedroom. In 1867, he bought Alaska from Russia for about $7.2 million, a deal critics mocked as “Seward’s Folly,” though Alaska later turned out to be rich in gold, oil, and fish.
topics.answerHtml: William Henry Seward (prompt on “William Henry” alone; do not accept “William Henry Harrison”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This man suggested a gentle closing for a speech, which Abraham Lincoln rewrote into the lines about “the mystic chords of memory” and “the better angels of our nature” at the end of his first inaugural address. Three years earlier, this man had called the struggle over slavery an “irrepressible conflict.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Yorker who served as Secretary of State and arranged the purchase of Alaska in 1867.

tossups.p: On April 1, 1861, this cabinet member sent the president a memo titled “Some Thoughts for the President’s Consideration,” suggesting that a war with a European power might reunite the country and offering to run the government’s policy himself. The president politely turned him down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Yorker who served as Secretary of State under Abraham Lincoln and Andrew Johnson.

tossups.p: Late in 1861, this official calmed a crisis with Britain by agreeing to release James Mason and John Slidell, two Confederate diplomats whom a U.S. Navy captain had seized from the British ship _Trent_. He explained that the captain had acted without orders.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Secretary of State who later bought Alaska from Russia.

tossups.p: In an 1850 Senate speech against compromising with slavery in the western lands, this New Yorker declared that “there is a higher law than the Constitution.” That speech opposed the package of bills that Henry Clay had proposed that year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this antislavery senator who later served as Abraham Lincoln’s Secretary of State.

tossups.p: In an 1858 speech in Rochester, this politician called the struggle over slavery “an irrepressible conflict between opposing and enduring forces.” That speech made him seem too radical to some Republicans, which helped cost him his party’s presidential nomination two years later.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New York senator who lost that nomination to Abraham Lincoln and then became his Secretary of State.

tossups.p: At the 1860 Republican convention in a Chicago hall called the Wigwam, this man led on the first two ballots, helped by his longtime political partner, the Albany editor Thurlow Weed. On the third ballot, the delegates turned to a rival from Illinois.
tossups.r: That rival was Abraham Lincoln. For 10 points, name this New Yorker who became Lincoln’s Secretary of State.

tossups.p: On April 5, 1865, this man broke his jaw and arm when he was thrown from his carriage. Nine days later, while he was still recovering in bed at his home near the White House, an attacker forced his way into the house.
tossups.r: That attacker, Lewis Powell, was part of John Wilkes Booth’s plot. For 10 points, name this Secretary of State who survived the attack and later bought Alaska.

tossups.p: This official negotiated a treaty with the Russian minister Eduard de Stoeckl that was signed on March 30, 1867. The deal cost the United States about 7.2 million dollars, or roughly two cents an acre.
tossups.r: Critics mocked that purchase of Alaska as this man’s “Folly.” For 10 points, name this Secretary of State.

tossups.p: In 1867, while this man was Secretary of State, the United States took possession of the Midway Islands in the Pacific, and he arranged a treaty to buy the Danish West Indies, though the Senate never approved it. That same year he made his most famous purchase.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Secretary of State under Lincoln and Andrew Johnson who bought Alaska from Russia in 1867.

tossups.p: After the Civil War, this diplomat pressured France to pull its troops out of Mexico, where Napoleon III had made the Austrian archduke Maximilian emperor. The French troops left by 1867, and Maximilian’s government soon collapsed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Secretary of State under Abraham Lincoln and Andrew Johnson who bought Alaska.

tossups.p: In 1859, this senator sold Harriet Tubman a house and land in Auburn, New York, where she later opened a home for elderly African Americans. This man lived in Auburn for most of his life and died there in 1872.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Yorker who served as Secretary of State and bought Alaska.

tossups.p: This man won his first election as an Anti-Masonic candidate for the New York State Senate, and he later served as a Whig governor of New York from 1839 to 1842. He was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1849.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Yorker who became Abraham Lincoln’s Secretary of State.

tossups.p: In July 1862, this cabinet member advised the president to wait until the Union won a major victory before announcing a plan to free enslaved people, so that it would not look like an act of desperation. The president waited until after Antietam.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Secretary of State who served under Abraham Lincoln and Andrew Johnson.

tossups.p: After leaving office in 1869, this man traveled around the world, a trip of more than a year. A state holiday on the last Monday in March, the peninsula that reaches closest to Russia, and a port city on the Kenai Peninsula all honor him.
tossups.r: Those places are in Alaska. For 10 points, name this Secretary of State who bought that territory from Russia in 1867.

tossups.p: This 1820 graduate of Union College was born in Florida, New York, and became a lawyer in Auburn. His wife, Frances, opened their Auburn home to freedom seekers on the Underground Railroad.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this New Yorker who later served as Abraham Lincoln’s Secretary of State and bought Alaska.

trap.title: Not the other William Henry
trap.body: Two famous Americans share the first names William Henry. William Henry Seward was the Secretary of State for Lincoln and Andrew Johnson who bought Alaska; William Henry Harrison was the ninth president, who won at Tippecanoe and died a month after taking office in 1841. Seward also gets mixed up with other members of Lincoln’s cabinet, such as Treasury Secretary Salmon Chase and War Secretary Edwin Stanton.
trap.fix: Alaska, the “higher law” and “irrepressible conflict” speeches, the _Trent_ Affair, Lewis Powell’s attack, and Auburn, New York, mean Seward. Saying just “William Henry” gets a prompt, so add “Seward.”
